fields.meta_title: Coffee Quiz: Find Your Roast, Then Build Your Own | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Take a free coffee quiz that matches you to a light, medium, or dark roast or to cold brew. Then build your own for a roastery, cafe, or club.
fields.h1: Build a Coffee Quiz That Matches Every Drinker to a Roast
fields.hero_description: Build a coffee quiz that matches each drinker to a roast, or take the eight-question one below to find yours.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Coffee Quiz
fields.features_subheading: One prompt builds the questions, the result screens, and the table every finish lands in. A second prompt changes any of them.
fields.feature_1:
Every option mapped to one roast

Name the roasts you sell as results. Emergent writes taste and habit questions, each option pointing at one of them, and a follow-up prompt rewords any question you dislike.
fields.feature_2:
Product picks on the result screen

Tag each bag you sell with one roast. The result screen lists the bags carrying that tag, with names and prices read from your store through its API, and a retag updates the quiz.
fields.feature_3:
A scored mode for barista training

Switch the quiz to scored for staff training: one option per question is marked correct, the app totals each score against your pass mark, and a miss shows the question it came from.
fields.feature_4:
Alerts the moment a quiz is finished

Send a Slack message or an email on every finish: the packer learns which roast to bag, the trainer reads the score the same morning. You choose who hears about which result.
fields.feature_5:
Results counted by month

A dashboard counts finished quizzes by result and by month, and a cold brew October becomes a stocking call. There is no response cap, however busy the holiday season gets.
fields.feature_6:
Runs on your domain, exports as code

Host the quiz on a custom domain, included in Emergent and billed in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and keep the questions in version control.

fields.usecase_heading: A Roaster, a Cafe, a Club, and a Training Bar
fields.tab_content_1:
Two bags wait on every Medium Roast result

Alderglen Roasters runs the coffee quiz on its online shop. Beatrix Duval finishes on Medium Roast, and her result screen shows the two bags tagged Medium, pulled from the store catalog. Her result and email land in the customer table.
fields.tab_content_2:
Cold brew won October and earned a second tap

Tin Whistle Cafe prints a QR code on every table, and each result names one drink from the menu. Owner Emeric Crespo opens the October dashboard: 412 finished quizzes, Cold Brew leading at 151. A second cold brew tap went on the bar before November.
fields.tab_content_3:
Milos's result goes into the first box

Perrine Coffee Club asks every new subscriber the quiz before checkout. Milos Dombrowski finishes on Dark Roast, the order for his first box is written with that roast, and packer Yael Quintana gets a Slack message naming the box and the roast to bag.
fields.tab_content_4:
Casper gets the espresso bar when he scores 9

Wrenhouse Coffee trains new baristas on a scored version: 10 brewing questions, pass mark of 8. Trainer Noriko Saito reads the scores the morning after each test. Casper Ricci scores 9 of 10, his row flips to cleared, and he takes the espresso bar that week.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Coffee Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create a coffee quiz that matches drinkers to a roast and saves every result, from picking results to testing each path.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the results before the questions
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask about the cup, not the bean
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Point every option at one result
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Tag each bag with one result
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start from what you sell or serve. A shop matches drinkers to roasts it stocks, a cafe to drinks on its menu, a trainer to a pass mark. This page's quiz uses four results: light, medium, dark, and cold brew. Every question has to sort takers among them.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Shoppers know how they drink, not how beans are processed. Ask about milk and sugar, the brew method at home, bitterness, and the time of their last cup. Skip anything a taker cannot answer from memory, such as origin or altitude.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write each answer choice so it clearly belongs to one roast, and keep the options in a set the same kind and length. An option that could mean two results muddies the match. Read every set aloud and check a stranger could guess which roast each option serves.
fields.howto_step_4_des: For a shop, tag every product with the roast it belongs to, and let the result screen list whatever carries the tag. Prices and names come from the store through its API, so a new bag joins its result the day you add it.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Send every finish to one table that keeps the answers and any email the taker leaves. Then route alerts from it, a Slack message to the packer or a morning score for the trainer, so nobody has to watch the table all day.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Add a scored version for training
fields.howto_step_6_des: A product finder has no wrong answers; a training quiz does. Mark one correct option per brewing question, set the pass mark, and show what a miss should have been. Keep each trainee's history so a retake is compared against the first run.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Take your own quiz before launch
fields.howto_step_7_des: Answer it once per result, aiming each run at one roast, and confirm the match lands where you expect. Then check the row it wrote, the alert it sent, and the products it listed. Fix the quiz by prompt and run the loop again.

faq_plan.a: A coffee quiz is a short set of questions that matches the taker to a coffee: a roast to buy, a drink to order, or the first bag in a subscription. Shops run it as a product finder, and a scored version tests brewing knowledge for training. The one above asks eight questions and matches four roasts.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a coffee quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe it to Emergent's AI survey builder: results first, then the questions, then where a finish should land. Emergent builds all three from the prompt and changes any of them when you ask again. The free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: What questions work best in a coffee quiz?
faq_plan.a: Picture questions beat jargon: a flavor you reach for, a cafe order, a weekend morning. Write them as choices between moments, not coffee terms, and give each roast one obvious home in every set of options. Keep the whole quiz under 10 questions, short enough to finish while the espresso pulls.

faq_plan.q: Where can I find coffee quiz questions and answers?
faq_plan.a: Write your own from a roast chart rather than a copied list, and every answer stays checkable. Dark roast beans are shiny black with an oily surface and a pronounced bitterness, and a lighter roast brews a more acidic cup. Pair each fact with three wrong options of the same kind. For a softer round, build it the way a love language quiz maps options to results.

faq_plan.q: How many results should a coffee quiz have?
faq_plan.a: Four results fit a coffee counter: one per roast depth, plus cold brew for the ice crowd. Add a fifth only when it changes what the taker is handed next, and cut any result that maps to nothing you sell or serve. More results also mean more tagging, since every product needs a home.

faq_plan.q: How do I show the right products on each coffee quiz result?
faq_plan.a: Give every product exactly one result tag, and let the screen do the rest. Three bags tagged Dark all show on a Dark Roast result, and an out-of-stock bag drops off the list because the store, not the quiz, holds the catalog. An Emergent quiz keeps each result and email in a database you own, where you can read which roast actually sells.

faq_plan.q: Can a coffee quiz be scored like a test?
faq_plan.a: Yes. A scored coffee quiz marks one correct option per question and totals the score against a pass mark, which fits barista training. A product finder works the other way, like a personality quiz: options map to results and nothing is wrong. Choose scored when a trainer reads the numbers, matching when a shopper does.

faq_plan.q: Should my coffee quiz ask for an email before the result?
faq_plan.a: Ask on the last screen, after the questions and before the reveal, when the taker has the most reason to trade it. Keep it optional for a cafe table quiz and required for a subscription, where the email ties the result to the first box. Each address lands beside its result, not in a separate list.

faq_plan.q: How do I track how many people finish my coffee quiz?
faq_plan.a: Count finishes on a dashboard split by result and by month. A month where cold brew leads is a stocking decision; a steep drop at one question tells you which one to rewrite. An Emergent quiz has no response caps: a busy season all gets counted.

faq_plan.q: What should a coffee quiz result screen say?
faq_plan.a: Name the match first, in the result's own words. Under it, one sentence on why the answers point there, then a single action: the bags to buy or the drink to order. The reveal works the way a spirit animal quiz does, and a restart beats a dead end for anyone who disagrees. Keep it short enough to read at a cafe table.

quiz.title: Which Coffee Roast Fits You?
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions about how you actually drink coffee. At the end you get one of four matches: light roast, medium roast, dark roast, or cold brew.

questions.text: How do you take your first cup of the day?

options.text: Black, and I want to taste everything
Strong enough to stand up to cream and sugar

questions.text: Pick one word for your ideal cup.
How do you brew at home?

options.text: Pour over, with the grounds weighed
A drip machine, same button every day
A pitcher steeping in the fridge

questions.text: When is your last coffee of the day?

options.text: Whenever, as long as it is cold

questions.text: How do you feel about bitterness?

options.text: I would rather taste fruit and florals
I avoid it where I can

questions.text: A cafe hands you the menu. What do you order?

options.text: Sweet enough to balance a strong cup

questions.text: What matters more when you buy a bag?

options.text: Where and how the beans were grown
A name I can reorder without thinking

results.title: Light Roast
results.description: Your answers lean toward bright, delicate cups taken black. Look for bags labeled light roast, brew them as pour over or drip, and hold the milk: the flavors you chase sit right at the surface of the cup.

results.title: Medium Roast
results.description: Your answers sit in the middle: balanced cups, a little milk, coffee at almost any hour. A bag labeled medium roast is your reorder, and it holds up in a drip machine, a French press, or a cappuccino.

results.title: Dark Roast
results.description: You picked bold, heavy, bitter-friendly answers. Reach for bags labeled dark or French roast and for espresso drinks, and do not apologize for the sugar: a dark cup carries it well.

results.title: Cold Brew
results.description: Your answers lean toward cold, smooth, slow-sipping cups. Order the cold brew on tap, and at home steep coarse grounds in the fridge overnight, then cut the concentrate with water or milk to taste.

quiz_plan.promise: the quiz plays the page's promise: a coffee quiz a visitor can take, whose results answer what the H1 says it builds

plan.angle: Eight of the top 10 are roasters' own bean finders and two are trivia lists, with no page that shows how to build one. A visitor can play an eight-question coffee quiz on this page that matches them to a light, medium, or dark roast or to cold brew, then see what four coffee businesses do with a result: an online roaster shows the bags tagged for it, a cafe names a menu drink and counts results by month, a subscription club sets the first box's roast, and a cafe trainer scores new baristas on a knowledge quiz. Every result lands in a database the owner keeps. The FAQ covers question writing, trivia answers, result count, product tagging, scoring, and length.
tab_stories: Teodora Vance takes the coffee quiz on Larchmont Roasters' shop, lands on Medium Roast, and her result screen shows the 2 bags the roaster tagged Medium, with her result and email saved to the customer table.

Copperleaf Cafe puts a QR code on every table, each of the 4 results names one drink on the menu, and owner Rafael Dunmore sees 412 finished quizzes in October with Cold Brew leading at 151, so he adds a second cold brew tap.

Saltmarsh Coffee Club asks every new subscriber the quiz before checkout, Wendell Ibarra's Dark Roast result sets the roast in his first box, and a Slack alert tells packer Noor Haddad to bag the dark roast.
Brightwater Coffee's trainer Jun Takeda gives each new barista a 10-question brewing test with a pass mark of 8, and Lena Whitcombe scores 9 of 10 and is cleared for the espresso bar.
